Once upon a time, Shark Tank India was about building startups.
Now, it’s about building hype and cashing out of it.

The same sharks who preached about honesty, valuation, and long-term vision are now using their Shark Tank fame to sell overpriced IPOs to the very public that trusted them.

Peyush Bansal (Lenskart) — the so-called “visionary founder” — is launching an IPO at a ₹70,000 crore valuation with a 260x PE ratio. Investors call it India’s most overrated IPO, full of overhype and underdelivery. Even franchise owners have accused Lenskart of hiding financial details and manipulating DRHP data. From startup inspiration to IPO exploitation — Peyush has turned Shark Tank’s credibility into a marketing weapon.

Aman Gupta (boAt) — the “cool marketer” of Shark Tank — is repeating the same playbook. After pulling back the IPO once, boAt is now pushing again for a listing around ₹13,000 crore valuation, despite falling profits, rising debts, and a Delhi High Court case against Boult Audio. It’s less about business now, more about selling the dream — a dream built on Shark Tank’s fame and audience trust.

Meanwhile, Vineeta Singh is openly frustrated with what the show has become. Ashneer Grover — the only shark who called out this hypocrisy — is out, and even his side ventures like Bhar Pee and CrickPe have failed. The sharks who once represented “India’s startup revolution” are now turning the tank into a circus of greed.

And what about Anupam Mittal? The self-proclaimed angel of ethics is busy taking indirect digs at other sharks on social media, proving how fractured this so-called “business brotherhood” really is.

The truth is simple — Shark Tank India has lost its soul.
What started as a platform for founders has become a launchpad for IPO frauds, PR stunts, and self-promotion.
The sharks aren’t investing anymore — they’re cashing out, using your trust as their exit plan.
